blocks.text: Optimizer state is the extra numeric information an optimizer maintains beyond the model weights themselves, running estimates that help it make smarter updates over time, and understanding exactly what this state contains and how much memory it costs closes out the practical picture behind every optimizer covered in this module.

This topic pulls together the state related details mentioned throughout the earlier SGD, Adafactor, and Lion topics into one focused explanation of what optimizer state actually is and why it matters so much for memory planning.
1. What Optimizer State Actually Contains
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101177-553693512.png

Beyond the model weights and the gradients computed at each training step, an optimizer often maintains additional numbers, tracked separately, that summarize information about recent gradients, this additional tracked information is what optimizer state refers to.
2. Why Optimizer State Exists At All

blocks.alt: Why Optimizer State Exists At All
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101178-906254673.png

Optimizer state exists because looking only at the current gradient, ignoring everything that happened in previous steps, throws away useful information, the momentum and adaptive learning rate mechanisms covered in the earlier Optimizers topic both rely on this remembered history to make smarter update decisions than a single current gradient alone could support.
3. Optimizer State for SGD, Minimal
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101449-325139429.png

Plain SGD, covered in the earlier dedicated topic, needs no additional state at all, it simply uses the current gradient directly. Adding momentum introduces exactly one additional tracked value per parameter, a running average of past gradient directions.
4. Optimizer State for Adam and AdamW, Larger

blocks.alt: Optimizer State for Adam and AdamW, Larger
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101450-336322895.png

Adam and AdamW maintain two separate running estimates per parameter, commonly called the first and second moment estimates, roughly tracking the average gradient direction and the average gradient magnitude respectively, which is why Adam optimizer state costs roughly twice as much memory as the model weights themselves.

code.content:
# A rough estimate of Adam optimizer state memory
def adam_state_memory(param_count, bytes_per_value):
    first_moment = param_count * bytes_per_value
    second_moment = param_count * bytes_per_value
    return first_moment + second_moment  # roughly 2x the weight memory

blocks.text: 5. Optimizer State Memory Relative to Model Weights

blocks.alt: Optimizer State Memory Relative to Model Weights
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101451-4116299.png

For a model trained with Adam, the optimizer state alone can require two to three times as much memory as the model weights themselves, once accounting for both moment estimates and, in full precision training, potentially higher precision copies of the state, a substantial addition worth planning for explicitly.

blocks.text: 6. Optimizer State and PEFT Methods
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101451-545754774.png

Because optimizer state scales with the number of trainable parameters, not the total model size, PEFT methods like LoRA, covered in the earlier dedicated module, dramatically reduce this specific memory cost as a direct side effect of training far fewer parameters than full fine-tuning would.

blocks.title: This closes the loop on several earlier topics at once
blocks.content: Optimizer state memory is exactly why choosing a PEFT method, a smaller optimizer like Adafactor, and quantizing the frozen base model all compound together into the combined memory savings covered in the Training Large Models on Limited GPUs topic.

blocks.text: 7. Saving and Restoring Optimizer State
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472101451-81911042.png

A full training checkpoint can optionally include optimizer state alongside the model weights, allowing training to resume exactly where it left off, with the same momentum and adaptive rate history intact, though many checkpoints saved purely for deployment purposes omit optimizer state entirely, since it is not needed for inference.
8. Optimizer State and Distributed Training

When training is spread across multiple devices, a topic covered in the Distributed Training Techniques module later in this course, optimizer state also needs to be distributed or synchronized correctly across those devices, adding another dimension of memory and coordination complexity beyond a single device training setup.
9. Choosing an Optimizer With State Size in Mind

Given how directly optimizer state size affects total memory usage, the choice between SGD, AdamW, Adafactor, and Lion, all covered in this module, is not purely about convergence speed or final quality, it is also a genuine memory planning decision, especially relevant when combined with the limited hardware considerations covered in the LoRA and QLoRA module.
Worked Example

A team calculates that their chosen base model has 7 billion parameters, and if they were to full fine-tune it with AdamW, the optimizer state alone would require roughly twice the memory of the weights themselves, well beyond their available hardware.

By fine-tuning with LoRA instead, training only a small fraction of the total parameters, their optimizer state shrinks proportionally, since AdamW only needs to track state for those few trainable LoRA parameters, not the entire frozen base model, making the combination of PEFT and a standard optimizer memory feasible where full fine-tuning never would have been.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to account for optimizer state memory when estimating total training memory requirements, focusing only on model weights
Assuming optimizer state size is fixed regardless of which optimizer is chosen, when it varies substantially between SGD, Adam, and Adafactor
Not recognizing that PEFT methods reduce optimizer state memory as a direct consequence of training fewer parameters
Saving unnecessary optimizer state in a deployment checkpoint meant purely for inference

blocks.text: Practice

For a model with a parameter count you choose, estimate the total memory needed for the weights, the gradients, and Adam optimizer state combined, confirming for yourself how much of the total memory budget optimizer state alone actually consumes.
Key Takeaway

Optimizer state is the additional tracked information, beyond weights and gradients, that optimizers like Adam maintain to make smarter updates over time, and because this state scales directly with the number of trainable parameters, it is a major reason PEFT methods, memory efficient optimizers like Adafactor, and careful optimizer choice all matter so much for fitting a fine-tuning run into limited hardware.
